newsitem.title: CHINA: Tibet rights groups reveals China famine cover-up.
newsitem.headline: Tibet rights groups reveals China famine cover-up.

text.p: A report by a major Tibetan religious leader kept secret by China for three decades shows Beijing covered up an official policy of famine and persecution in the remote region, a rights group said on Saturday.

The report by the late 10th Panchen Lama, the second holiest leader of the deeply devout Buddhist region, details mass arrests, political executions and man-made starvation in Tibet in the late 1950s and early 1960s.

The report, presented to Premier Zhou Enlai in May 1962, voiced fears that Chinese policies in Tibet were aimed at the eradication of religion and could lead to the elimination of Tibetans as a distinct people, said the London-based Tibet Information Network (TIN) which obtained the report.

The existence of the Panchen Lama's outspoken document has been known for years, but Tibet Information Network said this was the first time a full copy of the report, kept secret by Beijing authorities, had been obtained.

Written by the Panchen Lama after a tour to Tibet in 1961 and early 1962 from his base in Beijing, where he was required to live, the report hints a policy by China to eradicate religion could lead to serious unrest, if not rebellion.
The Panchen Lama, who died in 1989, spent 14 of the next 15 years after this report in detention or virtual house arrest.

Since the late 1980s, Tibet has been rocked by a series of sometimes violent demonstrations and riots led by monks and nuns against Chinese rule and for the return of their god-king, the Dalai Lama, who fled into exile after an abortive anti-Chinese uprising in 1959.

"We have no way of knowing how many have been arrested," the Panchen Lama wrote of the 1959 crackdown. "In each area 10,000 or more have been arrested. Good and bad, innocent or guilty, they have all been arrrested, contrary to any legal system that exists anywhere in the world."
He alleged a policy of collective punishment, with Tibetans executed because their relatives were involved in the uprising or subjected to persecution resulting in death.

The chief aim of the report appeared to be to persuade Beijing to stop starvation in Tibet in the early 1960s, when nearly 30 million Chinese died in a man-made famine after Chairman Mao Zedong launched his Great Leap Forward, TIN said.

"In some places, whole families have perished and the death rate is very high," the Panchen Lama wrote. "This is very abnormal, horrible and grave. In the past Tibet lived in a dark barbaric feudalism but there was never such a shortage of food, especially after Buddhism had spread."
The Panchen Lama warned that the policies in Tibet could lead to the annihilation of his people.
"The population of Tibet has been seriously reduced," he said. "It poses a grave danger to the existence of the Tibetan race and could even push the Tibetans to the last breath.
"The enlightenment-endowing Buddhist religion that flourishes throughout Tibet seems to be on the verge of being erased in front of our eyes from the land of Tibet," he said.
"There is no way that I and 90 percent of Tibetans will tolerate this," he warned.

The report was followed in the 1966-76 radical Cultural Revolution by the destruction and dynamiting of almost all monasteries in Tibet, although some are now being rebuilt and monks and Tibetans are allowed to worship freely.

However, a "special characteristics" concession adopted for Tibet by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping in the 1980s had been reversed in 1992 and followed by attempts to limit religious worship, appoint political loyalists to monastery committees and restrict Tibetan language teaching, TIN said.
Recent visitors to Tibet saw Tibetans worshipping freely at temples while monks engaged in their centuries-old religious ceremonies in monasteries.

However, the announcement late last year by Beijing of its discovery of a Chinese-anointed reincarnation of the Panchen Lama has aroused controversy after the Dalai Lama identified a reincarnation in May, 1995.
